patent: Filed 1935-10-30 and issued 1939-03-21 to Homer W. Dudley of Bell Telephone Laboratories. It is the basic patent on what Dudley later named the vocoder (voice coder), now called the channel vocoder: instead of the speech wave, the sending end transmits slowly varying measurements of it - the power in ten frequency bands from 250 to 7100 cycles, and the fundamental (pitch) frequency, or its absence for unvoiced sounds - and the receiving end rebuilds speech by shaping a local buzz (relaxation oscillator) or hiss (resistance noise) source through matching band filters. The patent puts the needed line band at about 360 cycles: twelve 20-cycle channels with 10-cycle guard spaces (ten for band power, one for pitch, one 60-cycle synchronizing pilot). It names the applications: narrow-band and submarine-cable telephony, secrecy (the line signal carries no intelligible speech), and altered voices (whisper from noise alone, chant from a fixed pitch). Dudley described the system in "Remaking speech", Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 1939. The vocoder principle was the speech-coding core of SIGSALY, the Allied secure telephone system in service from 1943, and the split of speech into an excitation source and a spectral envelope underlies later parametric speech coders.

figs.1: Whole two-way system, drawn sideways on the sheet. Each terminal joins its two-wire line to a four-wire loop through a hybrid coil (the coupled windings) with balancing network N. West to east runs along the top: compressing circuit 2 (detailed in FIG. 2), line L, restoring circuit 3 (detailed in FIG. 3), then 4 to the east hybrid; east to west runs along the bottom through 2', L' and 3'. Braces mark the bands: full speech band f_{1} to f_{2} at each end, narrow speech-defining band f'_{1} to f'_{2} on the lines, with f'_{2} - f'_{1} < f_{2} - f_{1}.
figs.2: Sending end (analyzer), speech entering at lower left. The input splits into FP (upper path) and AP; the top row is the pitch path: F_{0} (250-500 cycles), rectifier D, E_{1} and constant-output amplifier LA to isolate the fundamental, E_{2} and rectifier D_{0} to turn its frequency into a level, low-pass F_{30} (0-20), then modulator M_{0}, the only modulator drawn in detail (two tubes in push-pull inside the dash-dot box). Below, after delay equalizer DE, ten identical rows: band filter F_{n} (passband printed in each box), detector D_{n}, 20-cycle low-pass F_{30+n}, modulator M_{n} (drawn as a bare box), and channel filter C_{n} on the right. Oscillator O (60 cycles) drives multi-vibrator MV, whose 30-cycle harmonics are picked off by S_{0} to S_{10} (30, 90 ... 360 cycles) as carriers; each C_{n} keeps the lower side-band (10-30, 70-90 ... 340-360). C_{11} (40-60) passes the 60-cycle pilot. All channels join on the bus into transmitting amplifier TA and line L.
figs.3: Receiving end (synthesizer), line L entering at left through receiving amplifier RA. Bottom-left rows mirror FIG. 2: channel filters C'_{0} to C'_{10}, demodulators DM_{0} to DM_{10} (DM_{0} drawn as a rectifier bridge) fed with carriers from MV' through S'_{0} to S'_{10}, and low-pass filters F'_{30} to F'_{40} (boxes with arrows). MV' is locked to the sending oscillator by the 60-cycle pilot through C'_{11} and phase shifter PS. Top left, the excitation source: resistance R and amplifier A feed variable-gain amplifier VA, cut off by the pitch-channel bias at B_{1} during voiced sounds; the same bias at B_{2} sets the plate resistance of VR, which serves as resistance R_{0} timing multi-vibrator MV_{0} (the buzz), followed by equalizer E_{4}. Both outputs feed a common bus to band filters F'_{1} to F'_{10}; each band passes through shaping amplifier SN_{n} (only SN_{1} drawn in detail, gain set by bias resistor B_{3} from F'_{31}), whose gain follows the demodulated band power, then through F''_{n} into speech amplifier SA and out at 4.

parts.D_{0}: Converts the pitch frequency into a level: E_{2} ahead of it has loss that varies with frequency, so the rectified output tracks the fundamental frequency, not its amplitude.
parts.FPS: Drawing label for the dashed source box: resistance noise for unvoiced sounds; the multi-vibrator MV_{0} supplies the voiced (harmonic) excitation.
parts.R_{0}: Plate resistances of the two VR tubes in series; changing their grid bias changes the multi-vibrator frequency.
parts.C_{11}: Carries the 60-cycle oscillator tone to the receiving end so MV' generates carriers in step with MV.

glossary.def: Band-pass filter / low-pass filter; the box labels give the passband in cycles, the ~ sign marking alternating current.

Bridge transformer that splits a two-wire line into separate send and receive pairs (a four-wire circuit); balancing network N matches the line impedance so outgoing signal does not leak into the receive side.
Rectifier made of copper-oxide junctions, the common metal rectifier of the period; here it turns a band of speech into its envelope.
The slow rate, below about 10 to 20 cycles, at which speech power and pitch change as the vocal organs move.
Two-tube relaxation oscillator whose output is rich in harmonics; used as a carrier comb (MV, MV') and as the artificial vocal cords (MV_{0}).
Thermal (Johnson) noise of a resistor, a source with a continuous spectrum; stands in for the hiss of unvoiced sounds.
The patent's terms for, respectively, whether speech has a fundamental and what it is (pitch and voicing), and how power is spread over frequency (spectral envelope).
The band below the carrier produced by modulation; sending only one side-band (single side-band) halves the line band per channel.
Two tubes driven in opposite phase into a center-tapped transformer; biasing them together makes a balanced modulator or a gain-controlled amplifier.
Network that adds delay so the amplitude channels arrive in step with the slower pitch channel.
